chunks: Al-Husayn ibn Said from Safwan ibn Yahya and Ali ibn al-Nu'man from Sa'id ibn Yasar who said:

I said to Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him): A man performing Tamattu' walked between As-Safa and Al-Marwah six circuits, then returned to his home, believing he had finished, trimmed his nails, and emerged from Ihram. Later he remembered that he had walked only six circuits. He said to me: 'If he remembers that he walked six circuits, let him return and complete one circuit and offer a blood sacrifice.' I said: 'What blood?' He said: 'A cow.' He said: 'And if he does not remember that he walked six, let him return and begin the walking anew until he completes seven circuits, then offer the blood of a cow.'

key_terms.اَلصَّفَا: As-Safa, one of the two hills between which Sa'i is performed.
key_terms.اَلْمَرْوَةِ: Al-Marwah, the second hill in the Sa'i ritual.
key_terms.قَلَّمَ أَظْفَارَهُ: Trimmed his nails (an act that breaks Ihram).
key_terms.لْيُرِقْ دَماً: Let him shed/offer a blood sacrifice.
key_terms.مُتَمَتِّعٌ: A pilgrim who performs Umrah first, then Hajj, keeping Ihram intact or re-entering it.

ai.seo_question: What is the ruling for a pilgrim who completes only six circuits of Sa'i and exits Ihram?
ai.summary: This narration from *Tahdhib al-Ahkam* details the juristic distinction between intentional omission and honest mistake in the Sa'i ritual, emphasizing the Imam's precise criteria for validity based on the pilgrim's certainty (*yaqin*) versus doubt (*shakk*). The requirement of sacrificing a cow (*bakkara*) serves as a compensatory expiation (*kaffarah*) for the defect in the ritual, reflecting the Shia emphasis on ritual completeness (*itmam*) in Hajj. This ruling underscores the scholarly principle that acts of worship are judged by the state of mind and action at the time of completion, a key topic in Usul al-Fiqh regarding the validity of single vs. multiple acts.
